input: You sell 500 shares of a $40 stock at a broker with $0 commissions. Which regulatory fees do you still pay on this sell, and roughly how much (2026 rates)?
expected_output: Two sell-side pass-throughs: the SEC Section 31 fee at $20.60 per $1,000,000 of notional (500 × $40 = $20,000 → about $0.41) and the FINRA Trading Activity Fee at $0.000195 per share (500 shares → about $0.10, capped at $9.79 per trade). Buys pay neither. Rates reset periodically — the SEC rate changes each fiscal year.

input: Why does a 'commission-free' market order still cost you money the moment it fills, and how large is that cost for a liquid large-cap vs a small-cap?
expected_output: A marketable order crosses the bid-ask spread: you buy at the ask and sell at the bid, paying roughly half the quoted spread each way versus the mid. For mega-cap stocks and major ETFs that's on the order of 1–5 basis points; small caps commonly run 20–100 bps, and spreads widen further at the open/close and in extended hours. Round trip, you pay the half-spread twice — plus slippage.

input: In a cash account you sell stock on Monday morning and immediately buy a different stock with the proceeds, then sell that new stock the same afternoon. What rule have you violated and why?
expected_output: A good-faith violation. Equity sales settle T+1, so Monday's proceeds don't become settled funds until Tuesday; buying with unsettled proceeds is allowed only if you hold the new position until those funds settle. Selling it Monday afternoon — before the funding sale settles — means you traded with money you never actually had. Waiting until the settlement date (Tuesday) to sell would have been compliant. Repeated GFVs (typically 2–3 in 12 months) get the account restricted to settled-funds-only for 90 days.

input: Does the Pattern Day Trader $25,000 minimum still apply in 2026?
expected_output: No. The PDT designation and $25k minimum were abolished effective June 4, 2026, replaced by an intraday margin standard under FINRA Rule 4210 (phasing in through 2027). Day-trading margin mechanics still exist, and cash accounts are still bound by settled-funds rules — only the $25k/PDT-label framework was retired.

input: A strategy wins 70% of the time. Is it profitable?
expected_output: Unknowable from win rate alone. Profitability is expectancy: (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss) − costs. A 70% winner that makes 1R on wins and loses 3R on losses has negative expectancy; a 35% winner with 3R wins and 1R losses is strongly positive. Net expectancy after spread, slippage, and fees is the only number that matters.

input: What is an R-multiple and why does the paper broker require a stop price on every entry?
expected_output: R is the initial risk on the trade: (entry − stop) × quantity. Outcomes are expressed as multiples of that risk — a +2R trade made twice what it risked. Without a stop there is no defined R, so position sizing under a fixed-fractional risk rail (e.g. risk 1% of equity per trade) is impossible and outcomes can't be compared across trades.

input: You sell AAPL at a loss and buy it back a week later. What happens to that loss for tax purposes?
expected_output: It's a wash sale: a loss is disallowed when you acquire substantially identical securities within 30 days before or after the sale (a 61-day window). The disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement shares — deferred, not destroyed. For a bot that rapidly re-enters the same symbols, tax P&L can diverge badly from mark-to-market P&L, and a December loss re-entered in January defers the deduction a full year.

input: What does a small retail account actually pay per side to trade BTC on a mainstream US venue in 2026?
expected_output: On Coinbase Advanced Trade at the base tier (<$10k 30-day volume) roughly 0.60% taker / 0.40% maker per side, plus the book spread (1–5 bps on BTC/ETH). Kraken Pro's base tier is 0.40%/0.25%. 'Simple buy' retail flows cost more — about a 0.5% spread markup plus flat fees. Round trip at base tier, fees alone are over 1% — a huge hurdle for short-horizon trading.

input: Your stop is at $95 and the stock closes at $98, then opens the next day at $88 on bad news. Where does your stop-loss order fill?
expected_output: At (or near) the $88 open — not at $95. A stop becomes a market order when the stop price is touched or gapped through; overnight gaps fill at the next available price. Realistic simulation and honest risk math must assume gap risk: the stop defines intended risk, not guaranteed maximum loss.

input: Name three ways paper-trading results systematically flatter a strategy compared to live trading.
expected_output: (1) Fill assumptions: sims fill at last/mid or on a touch, while real market orders cross the spread and real limit orders need price to trade through (or deep queue priority). (2) No partial fills or latency: real fast markets slip beyond the quote and fill in pieces. (3) Missing costs: regulatory fees, widened spreads at open/close and after hours, borrow costs, margin interest. A strategy profitable with perfect fills can lose with realistic execution — which is why net-of-costs paper results and sim-vs-real drift tracking matter.
